proof:
Source: P. Mattila, Geometry of Sets and Measures in Euclidean Spaces, Theorem 18.5. This is a density theorem of Mickle and Radó: if ψ is a measure on ℝᵏ and A is Lᵏ-measurable with ψ(A) = 0, then for Lᵏ-a.e. x ∈ A, limsup_{r↓0}r^{−k}ψ(B(x,r)) ∈ {0,∞}. It is the version cited by Hovila-Järvenpää-Järvenpää-Ledrappier (arXiv:1104.3453, proof of Lemma 2.4); see also P. Mattila, Rectifiability: a survey (arXiv:2112.00540), Lemma 4.14 ('a simple covering argument combined with Lebesgue density theorem'). That argument is written out below. The inner continuity of ψ on open balls is used only to make the sets involved Borel.

Notation: B(c,τ) is the open ball in ℝᵏ, k := m + 1, ω_k := Lᵏ(B(0,1)), f_c(t) := ψ(B(c,t))/tᵏ for t > 0, and ϑ(c) = limsup_{t↓0}f_c(t).

1. Measurability. For τ > 0 the map c ↦ ψ(B(c,τ)) is lower semicontinuous. Indeed, let c_l → c and 0 < τ′ < τ. Then B(c,τ′) ⊆ B(c_l,τ) as soon as |c_l − c| < τ − τ′, so ψ(B(c,τ′)) ≤ liminf_lψ(B(c_l,τ)). Taking the supremum over τ′ ∈ (0,τ) and using the hypothesis ψ(B(c,τ)) = sup_{τ′<τ}ψ(B(c,τ′)) gives ψ(B(c,τ)) ≤ liminf_lψ(B(c_l,τ)).
 For q ∈ ℕ, q ≥ 1, let g_q(c) := sup_{0<t<1/q}f_c(t). As a supremum of lower semicontinuous functions, g_q is lower semicontinuous, hence Borel. Moreover g_q ↓ ϑ pointwise as q → ∞, since ϑ(c) = inf_qg_q(c) by the definition of limsup. Hence ϑ is Borel.

2. Reduction. For q ≥ 1 let S_q := {c ∈ D : ϑ(c) > 1/q and g_q(c) ≤ q}. This is a Borel set, since {g_q ≤ q} is closed.
 Let c ∈ D with 0 < ϑ(c) < ∞. Since inf_qg_q(c) < ∞, g_{q₀}(c) < ∞ for some q₀, and g_q is non-increasing in q. So every q ≥ max(q₀, g_{q₀}(c)) with 1/q < ϑ(c) satisfies c ∈ S_q.
 Hence {c ∈ D : 0 < ϑ(c) < ∞} ⊆ ⋃_qS_q, and it suffices to show Lᵏ(S_q) = 0 for each q.

3. Lᵏ(S_q) = 0. Fix q and suppose Lᵏ(S_q) > 0.
 By inner regularity of Lebesgue measure there is a compact K ⊆ S_q with Lᵏ(K) > 0. Lebesgue's density theorem (Mathlib Besicovitch.ae_tendsto_measure_inter_div) gives Lᵏ(K ∩ B̄(c,ρ))/Lᵏ(B̄(c,ρ)) → 1 as ρ ↓ 0 for (Lᵏ⌞K)-a.e. c. Since Lᵏ(K) > 0, such a point c₀ ∈ K exists. Since Lᵏ(∂B(c₀,ρ)) = 0, Lᵏ(B(c₀,ρ)∖K)/Lᵏ(B(c₀,ρ)) = 1 − Lᵏ(K ∩ B̄(c₀,ρ))/Lᵏ(B̄(c₀,ρ)) → 0 as ρ ↓ 0.
 Let ε := 1/(2q²12ᵏ). Choose t₀ > 0 with Lᵏ(B(c₀,2t)∖K) ≤ εω_k(2t)ᵏ for 0 < t < t₀, and with 12ε^{1/k}t₀ < 1/q. Since c₀ ∈ S_q, ϑ(c₀) > 1/q, so there is t ∈ (0,t₀) with ψ(B(c₀,t)) > tᵏ/q.
 Because K ⊆ S_q ⊆ D and ψ(D) = 0, ψ(K) = 0, so ψ(B(c₀,t)) ≤ ψ(B(c₀,t)∖K) + ψ(K) = ψ(B(c₀,t)∖K).
 For z ∈ B(c₀,t)∖K let d(z) := dist(z,K). Since K is closed and c₀ ∈ K, 0 < d(z) ≤ |z − c₀| < t. The open ball B(z,d(z)) does not meet K and is contained in B(c₀,2t). Hence ω_kd(z)ᵏ ≤ Lᵏ(B(c₀,2t)∖K) ≤ εω_k(2t)ᵏ, i.e. d(z) ≤ 2ε^{1/k}t.
 By the Vitali covering lemma (enlargement factor 2, as in Mathlib Vitali.exists_disjoint_subfamily_covering_enlargement) there are countably many points z_i ∈ B(c₀,t)∖K such that the balls B(z_i,d_i), d_i := d(z_i), are pairwise disjoint and B(c₀,t)∖K ⊆ ⋃_iB(z_i,5d_i).
 Since K is compact, choose z′_i ∈ K with |z_i − z′_i| = d_i. Then B(z_i,5d_i) ⊆ B(z′_i,6d_i) and 6d_i ≤ 12ε^{1/k}t < 1/q. So g_q(z′_i) ≤ q gives ψ(B(z′_i,6d_i)) ≤ q(6d_i)ᵏ. The disjoint balls B(z_i,d_i) lie in B(c₀,2t)∖K. Therefore
 ψ(B(c₀,t)∖K) ≤ Σ_iψ(B(z′_i,6d_i)) ≤ q6ᵏΣ_id_iᵏ = q6ᵏω_k^{−1}Σ_iLᵏ(B(z_i,d_i)) ≤ q6ᵏω_k^{−1}Lᵏ(B(c₀,2t)∖K) ≤ q6ᵏε(2t)ᵏ = tᵏ/(2q).
 This contradicts ψ(B(c₀,t)) > tᵏ/q. Hence Lᵏ(S_q) = 0, and Lᵏ({c ∈ D : 0 < ϑ(c) < ∞}) ≤ Σ_qLᵏ(S_q) = 0. ∎
key_steps: Inner continuity on balls makes c ↦ ψ(B(c,τ)) lower semicontinuous, so g_q(c) = sup_{0<t<1/q}ψ(B(c,t))/tᵏ and ϑ = inf_q g_q are Borel.
{c ∈ D : 0 < ϑ(c) < ∞} ⊆ ⋃_q S_q, where the Borel sets S_q := {c ∈ D : ϑ(c) > 1/q, g_q(c) ≤ q} carry the uniform upper bound ψ(B(c,τ)) ≤ qτᵏ for τ < 1/q.
If Lᵏ(S_q) > 0, take a compact K ⊆ S_q and a Lebesgue density point c₀ ∈ K. Since ψ(K) ≤ ψ(D) = 0, ψ(B(c₀,t)) = ψ(B(c₀,t)∖K).

Cover B(c₀,t)∖K by Vitali balls B(z,dist(z,K)), whose radii are small because c₀ is a density point. The enlarged balls centred in K have ψ-mass ≤ q(6d)ᵏ, so ψ(B(c₀,t)) ≤ tᵏ/(2q), contradicting ϑ(c₀) > 1/q.
